name: Model Evaluation and Drift
intent: Measure whether a model, prompt or retrieval change made answers better or worse, with enough data to tell a real change from noise, and keep measuring after it ships.
scenario: A support assistant team wants to ship a new prompt on a cheaper model. A golden set of 200 graded questions says the pass rate moves from 70.0% to 73.5%. Is that real? The change is gated in CI, shadowed and canaried on live traffic, and three weeks later the questions people ask have drifted away from the golden set.
problem: Model behaviour cannot be checked with unit tests: the output differs from run to run, there is rarely one right answer, and a change that fixes some prompts quietly breaks others. Teams then ship on a handful of eyeballed examples, or trust a score from a small eval set whose noise is larger than the effect they are measuring. After release the world moves (new topics, new phrasing, new upstream data) and a model that passed every test slowly gets worse with no deploy to blame.

howItWorks.title: Build a golden set and grade it with rubrics
howItWorks.text: Collect a few hundred to a few thousand real prompts (sampled from production, with the hard and rare cases deliberately over-represented) and write down what a good answer must do: contains the refund policy, cites a source, does not invent an order number. Grading is pass/fail per rubric item, exact match or a checker where an answer is checkable, and a model or a human where it is not. Accuracy, precision and recall apply to anything with a label (did it route to the right queue); free text gets a pass rate on rubrics. Split by slice (language, intent, customer tier) so a drop in one slice is not hidden by the average.

howItWorks.title: Use an LLM as the judge, then calibrate it against humans
howItWorks.text: A judge model scores thousands of answers cheaply, but it has known biases: it prefers the answer shown first (position), the longer one (verbosity) and text that looks like its own (self-preference). Mitigate by randomising or swapping order and scoring both, grading against a rubric rather than asking which is better, and not letting a model judge its own family. Then measure the judge: have humans label a sample of 50 to 200 items, compute agreement (and Cohen's kappa, since 80% agreement on a 90% pass rate is barely better than chance), and re-check whenever the judge model or rubric changes.

howItWorks.title: Compare old and new on the same items, with an interval
howItWorks.text: Run both versions on the identical items and look at the per-item difference: items the new version fixed (+1), broke (-1) and left alone (0). Only the discordant items carry information, so the paired interval is far narrower than comparing two independent pass rates. The standard error of the mean difference gives a 95% interval of about plus or minus 1.96 standard errors; a bootstrap over items gives a similar one without the normal assumption. Interval width falls with the square root of the set size: 4 times the items halves it. With a 200-item set and a 70% pass rate the interval is typically 5 to 9 points wide, so a 2 point change is invisible.

howItWorks.title: Gate the change in CI before it ships
howItWorks.text: Wire the eval into the pull request: a prompt, model, retrieval or tool change must run the suite and meet a rule written down in advance, for example 'the lower bound of the pass-rate difference must be above -2 points, and no slice may drop more than 5 points'. Pin the model version and the judge version, set temperature to 0 or run each item several times, cache unchanged items, and keep the suite fast enough that people do not skip it. The gate decides whether a change is safe to try on traffic; it rarely proves a change is better.

howItWorks.title: Shadow, canary and watch the live signals
howItWorks.text: Offline sets lag reality, so check live: shadow the candidate on a copy of real requests and compare answers without showing them, then serve it to 1 to 5% of users behind a feature flag and watch thumbs-down rate, escalations, refusals, latency and cost against an SLO. Monitor drift separately: input drift (the mix of topics, lengths and languages versus your golden set), output drift (answer length, refusal rate, format failures) and feedback. Sample failing live traces back into the golden set, and keep rollback to a flag flip so a bad model is gone in minutes, not a release.

pros: Turns 'it feels better' into a number with an error bar, so arguments about prompts end faster
Catches regressions in untouched behaviour before users do, because every change runs the whole suite
A calibrated judge makes thousands of free-text answers gradeable for the price of a few API calls
Live monitoring finds slow decay that no deploy caused
The golden set doubles as a regression record: each production bug becomes a permanent test
cons: Building and labelling a good golden set is real work, and it needs a domain expert more than an ML engineer
Judge models are biased and drift when the provider updates them; the judge needs its own tests
Small sets produce noisy verdicts, large sets cost money and time on every pull request
Offline scores and user happiness correlate only loosely, so a green gate is not a launch decision
Everything must be versioned (prompt, model, retrieval index, judge, dataset) or numbers cannot be compared
whenToUse: Any user-facing LLM feature where a prompt, model or retrieval change can alter answers
Classification or ranking models with labels, where accuracy, precision and recall can be tracked per slice
Before swapping to a cheaper or faster model, where the question is whether quality held
Long-running systems whose inputs change over time
whenNotToUse: A prototype whose behaviour is changing daily: ten hand-read examples per change are cheaper than a harness
Fully deterministic steps (parsing, arithmetic, schema validation): ordinary unit tests are sharper
As the only safety control: it measures average quality and does not replace guardrails against adversarial input
Chasing a metric the eval set no longer represents: optimising a stale set makes the score rise and users unhappier
pitfalls: Declaring a win from a 100 item set with a 12 point wide interval: the measured gap was luck
Leakage: golden prompts end up in the prompt's few-shot examples, a fine-tuning set or the retrieval index, and the score rises without the model improving
Re-running the eval and tweaking the prompt until it passes, which is multiple testing against one set; hold out a second set for the final check
Judge and candidate from the same model family, so self-preference inflates the score
Judging with a different rubric version than last week and comparing the two numbers anyway
Averaging over slices: overall pass rate +1 point while the refunds slice falls 25 points
Treating a drift alert as an outage when it only means the traffic mix changed; check quality on the new traffic before rolling back

roles.label: Candidate change
roles.description: A new prompt, model, retrieval setting or tool definition proposed in a pull request.

roles.label: Golden set
roles.description: Versioned graded prompts with rubrics, sliced by intent, plus a human-labelled calibration sample.

roles.label: Judge
roles.description: A model or human that grades answers against a rubric; itself measured against human labels.

roles.label: Release gate
roles.description: Computes the paired difference and its interval and applies a rule fixed in advance.

roles.label: Live monitor
roles.description: Shadow and canary traffic, drift and feedback metrics, and the flag that rolls back.
